progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: chem-m6-c05 (strong and weak as complete and partial ionisation; ethanoic/acetic acid stops early at equilibrium; the single and double arrow; NaOH a strong base, ammonia a weak base; concentration is a separate quantity; a concentrated weak acid can read lower than a dilute strong one; compare strength at the same concentration; diluting a weak acid lets a bigger fraction ionise; lower pH means more hydronium, one unit is ten times). chem-m6-p03 (the pH meter routine: calibrate with buffers covering the readings, rinse and blot, wait for steady, three readings in fresh portions; the 0.010 mol/L readings HCl 2.03, acetic acid 3.40, ammonia 10.59, NaOH 11.96). chem-m5-p01 (validity, reliability, accuracy; variables; risk as hazard, harm, control). Module 5 equilibrium (a reversible reaction settles at a balance; a reverse step that needs two dissolved particles to meet slows more on dilution, so the balance shifts toward the side with more dissolved particles; used in scene 9). Year 11 Module 2 (concentration in mol/L; dilution, c₁V₁ = c₂V₂; volumetric pipette and flask). Not assumed: pH = −log[H₃O⁺], pOH, Kw, Ka, Kb, conjugate pairs.
progression.startsWith: Prepare equal-concentration strong and weak comparison solutions. The video opens: Two bottles, both labelled zero point one zero zero moles per litre. One's hydrochloric acid, the other's ethanoic acid. You've only got a pH meter.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining why strength must be compared at matched concentration; carrying out the matched comparison and explaining the pH gap by extent of ionisation; designing and carrying out a tenfold dilution with volumetric glassware; explaining why a strong acid's pH rises by about one unit and a weak acid's by much less (about half for ethanoic acid), and that the bases mirror this; naming the variables; judging validity, reliability and accuracy; writing the risk rows. No pH calculation (chem-m6-c07), no Ka or Kb (chem-m6-c10), no conjugate pairs (chem-m6-c06), no conductivity.
progression.nextLesson: conjugate pairs and amphiprotic species: why chloride never takes its proton back but ethanoate does (route chem-m6-c06).

teaching.task: Two bottles, both labelled 0.100 mol/L: one hydrochloric acid, one ethanoic acid. How can a pH meter show which acid is strong, what makes the comparison fair, and how could you still tell them apart if you couldn't trust the label?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) two acids labelled 0.100 mol/L: which is strong, and could a wrong label fool you? (1); (2) same concentration, so any pH difference comes from strength; a concentrated weak acid can read lower than a dilute strong one (C05), so unmatched solutions prove nothing; P03 used this test at 0.010 mol/L, and this time all four are at 0.100 mol/L (2); (3) the P03 routine, plus a note that readings near 1 and 13 sit outside the 4 to 10 calibration (3); (4) results: HCl 1.08 against ethanoic acid 2.90; NaOH 12.91 against ammonia 11.10 (4); (5) at the same concentration, HCl has about 70 times as much hydronium (two units would be 100 times; 1.82 units is a bit less), because every HCl molecule ionises and only a small fraction of ethanoic acid molecules do (C05, with the arrows recalled); the bases mirror it (5); (6) but this relies on the label; the dilution test: 10.00 mL made up to 100.0 mL is exactly tenfold, whatever the starting concentration (6); (7) results: HCl and NaOH move 0.96, almost exactly one unit; ethanoic acid and ammonia about 0.50 (7); (8) a strong acid is already fully ionised, so diluting tenfold leaves a tenth of the hydronium per litre: about one pH unit (8); (9) diluted, the hydronium and ethanoate ions meet less often, so fewer rejoin into molecules and a bigger fraction of the acid stays ionised, which partly makes up the loss, so hydronium falls by much less than ten times: about half a unit (9); (10) the bases mirror this; the diluted readings match P03's 0.010 mol/L readings; the acid gap narrows from 1.82 to 1.35 units on dilution, which is why P03 found about 23 times, not 70 (10); variables (11); validity, reliability, accuracy (12); risk (13); memory aid (14); attempts and brief feedback (15 to 18); decision rule and handoff (19); key notes (20).
teaching.conversationalApproach: two bottles both labelled 0.100 mol/L hold hydrochloric and ethanoic acid, and the practical asks how a pH meter can show which is strong, and what to do if a label might be wrong. Test 1 compares at the same concentration because a concentrated weak acid can read a lower pH than a dilute strong one; the P03 routine is reused, and one class's means are read as about seventy times as much hydronium. Test 2 dilutes exactly tenfold with a volumetric pipette and flask: the strong acid rises about one unit because the same ions are spread through ten times the volume, and the weak acid only about half because more molecules ionise when the ions meet less often; the bases mirror this and the readings agree with P03. The variables, validity, reliability and accuracy, and the risk assessment follow, and the memory aid is "Match, then compare. Dilute ten times: strong moves about one, weak moves about half." Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: Two bottles, both labelled zero point one zero zero moles per litre. One's hydrochloric acid, the other's ethanoic acid. You've only got a pH meter. Can you show which acid is strong? And here's the harder part: what if one label is wrong? Today you'll build two pH tests of strength, and the second one doesn't trust the label at all.
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A student wants to compare the strengths of methanoic acid (HCOOH) and nitric acid (HNO₃). Using a calibrated pH meter at 25 °C, she measures the pH of 0.50 mol/L methanoic acid as 2.03 and the pH of 0.0020 mol/L nitric acid as 2.70. She concludes that methanoic acid is the stronger acid. Evaluate her conclusion and describe how she should change her method." Answer: the conclusion is not valid: the concentrations differ by 250 times, so the pH depends on concentration as well as strength; test both at the same concentration (for example 0.100 mol/L), same temperature and meter; nitric acid, which ionises completely, would then read lower. Crossed mistake: "lower pH, so stronger acid". (A2) "A student has a solution of a monoprotic acid of unknown concentration. Its pH is 2.40. She uses a volumetric pipette to transfer 10.00 mL of it into a 100.0 mL volumetric flask and makes it up to the mark with distilled water. The diluted solution has a pH of 2.90. Determine whether the acid is strong or weak. Justify your answer." Answer: weak: a tenfold dilution of a strong acid leaves a tenth of the hydronium, raising the pH by about 1 (to about 3.4); it rose by only 0.50, so hydronium fell by much less than ten times; more molecules ionised on dilution, which only happens with partial ionisation. Crossed mistake: "pH 2.40 is low, so it's a strong acid".
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct an investigation to demonstrate the use of pH to indicate the differences between the strength of acids and bases (ACSCH102)" this video prepares students to carry out and analyse the strength investigation; it does not claim that watching it is conducting it. It teaches two pH tests of strength: (1) the matched comparison: a strong and a weak acid (and a strong and a weak base) at the same concentration, 0.100 mol/L, so the pH gap comes from how completely each ionises; (2) the tenfold dilution test: dilute each solution exactly tenfold with volumetric glassware and watch how far the pH moves (strong acid about one unit, weak acid about half a unit; the bases mirror this), which does not depend on trusting the label's concentration. It also covers the variables, validity, reliability and accuracy, and the risk assessment. Placement limits (playlist order 8): this video comes before conjugate pairs (chem-m6-c06, order 9), pH calculation (chem-m6-c07, order 10), ICE tables (chem-m6-c08, order 12) and Ka (chem-m6-c10, order 14). So no pH is calculated from a concentration, no Ka or Kb appears, and the half-unit result for the weak acid is explained with C05's particle idea only (diluting a weak acid lets a bigger fraction of its molecules ionise), not derived. The pH meter routine (calibrate, rinse, blot, wait for steady, three readings in fresh portions) is P03's and is recalled in one scene, not re-taught. The particle model of strong against weak, the arrows and the "concentrated weak can read lower than dilute strong" surprise are C05's and are recalled, not re-taught. Conductivity is not used (open decision).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout (C01, C05, P03): hydronium teal, hydroxide violet; whole acid molecules amber outline; readout amber digits; acids marked with a small teal tab on their beaker labels, bases a violet tab; strong solutions' change bars solid, weak solutions' change bars outlined; controls green, hazards terracotta. Board layout (three zones, constant): top-left the short task line; the centre holds the meter and the beaker row (or the dilution glassware); the right third holds the current card (method recall, results, variables, VRA, risk), one at a time. Clutter rule: at most three bright text items; every tag dims when its sentence ends. Reuse: `m6-ph-meter-probe-beaker-v1.png` (inspected for P03 on 21 Oct: bench meter with a blank green screen, probe on a cable in a beaker of clear liquid; coded amber readout in the screen), `m6-beaker-v1.png` (empty clear beaker; eight coded copies across scenes 2 and 6), `m6-volumetric-pipette-filler-v1.png` (inspected 21 Oct: bulb pipette with a red pipette filler, tip down at an angle; used at native aspect, rotated as a whole only), `m6-volumetric-flask-v1.png` (inspected 21 Oct: stoppered volumetric flask with a calibration mark on the neck; a coded fill rises to the mark), `m6-wash-bottle-v1.png` (rinse recall and making up to the mark), `m5x-safety-glasses-v1.png` (risk table), `m5x-ammonia-bottle-v1.png` (risk row, the stock bottle, small, "teacher only"), `m6-buffer-bottle-v1.png` (three calibration buffers, as in P03), `m6-ph-probe-holder-v1.png` and `m6-lab-tissue-v1.png` (P03 recall). The last three are P03's Codex asset brief items 1 to 3, not yet painted; this video needs them only if P03's brief is delivered first, and its scene 3 can fall back to the meter plate alone. No human figures.
